newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African town "frees" Mandela 34 years on.
newsitem.headline: S.African town "frees" Mandela 34 years on.

text.p: For the first time since his release from prison six years ago, President Nelson Mandela on Thursday visited the South African site where apartheid police officers arrested him three decades ago.

Tweedie, a village near the town of Howick in KwaZulu-Natal province, is where Mandela -- branded The Black Pimpernel at the time -- was arrested on August 5, 1962, for public incitement and planning a violent overthrow of the apartheid state.
When he was arrested, Mandela was driving back to Johannesburg from a secret African National Congress meeting he had attended in Durban, without realising the police were on his trail.
From there he went to detention, trial and imprisonment for life, which in fact lasted until 1990 when South Africa's last white president F.W. de Klerk released him.

Sporting an elegant brown shirt, Mandela first walked around what was then a dusty road, but now tarred and surrounded by lush gum-tree plantations, before shaking hands with locals who came to see him unveil a plaque recalling his arrest.
He told the crowd his arrest had been professional.
"The policemen of Natal in the 50s and 60s were people who were proud of the good name of the police and who maintained the highest standard of professionalism," he said.
Some villagers said they had had no idea Mandela had been arrested on their doorstep. The president was given the freedom of Howick award to mark his visit.
"We are here to give Mandela his freedom because he lost it here. He is a man who fought for humanity and should not even have been arrested," said local man David Hlela, 35.

Mandela, 78, said he harboured no animosity against the officers who handcuffed him, and that his only regret was that he had not been able to meet again a 'Sergeant Vorster' who had told him politely he was being arrested.

"The only regret I have is that I have not been able to see that officer and to say to him let bygones be bygones and to shake hands with him and to say I hope the South African Police Sevice will follow his example."
Mandela later went on to address Howick city councillors who officially conferred upon him the award on him.
